periods.analysis: We begin this cycle in a yellow posture: chronic absenteeism is 18%, above our <=15 target, and school safety incidents are 7 per 1,000 students against a <=5 target. At the same time, K-12 Enrollment is a strong 244000 students, above the >=240000 target, which tells me families are still choosing our schools even while the daily experience needs tighter execution. The first attendance review of the year showed the heaviest misses in the East Harbor Grade 6-9 cohort and along the late-running Route 14 and Route 22 bus corridors. Our principals are not treating this as a paperwork issue; they are treating it as a relationship, transportation, and campus-climate issue.
periods.recommendations: Hold the yellow line by launching weekly attendance huddles at the 25 highest-absence campuses, with named student lists reviewed every Monday by principals, counselors, and family liaisons. Sustain the green enrollment result by extending the Welcome Harborview enrollment desk at Airport Gateway, Dockside, and Southpoint through the first 30 instructional days. For safety, deploy the Safe Passage teams to the Route 14 and Route 22 arrival windows and require incident debriefs within 48 hours at any campus above 8 per 1,000.

periods.analysis: The quarter is still yellow, but the shape changed: chronic absenteeism moved up from 18% to 18.8%, while K-12 Enrollment eased from 244000 to 242200 students and remains green above the >=240000 target. Safety incidents improved slightly from 7 to 6.8 per 1,000 students, which is welcome, but we are still not at the <=5 standard our students deserve. The December data point was pulled down by illness spikes after the fall respiratory wave and by recurring Friday absences at Bayview, Mariner, and Portside middle schools. I see disciplined work in the safety numbers, but attendance is now the watch-item that must not become normalized.
periods.recommendations: Keep the campus safety playbook in place and extend the Mariner Hallway Reset model to Bayview and Portside, including staggered passing periods and adult posts at B-wing and cafeteria doors. For attendance, open a winter recovery sprint focused on students with 6 to 10 absences, using text nudges from the ParentSquare vendor and home visits by bilingual liaisons before the break. Protect enrollment by calling every family in pending-transfer status within five business days and offering same-week placement support at the Central Enrollment counter.

periods.analysis: We remain yellow, and the attendance trend is moving the wrong way: chronic absenteeism rose from 18.8% to 19.5%, now 4.5 points above the <=15 target. K-12 Enrollment declined from 242200 to 240500 students, still green but only 500 students above the >=240000 floor, so the margin has narrowed. Safety incidents improved again from 6.8 to 5.9 per 1,000 students, showing that the climate work is taking hold even though it remains above the <=5 target. The strongest safety gains came at Lincoln Prep and Harbor Tech after we added morning door teams and the Navigate360 reporting refresh.
periods.recommendations: Stay with the safety work and sustain the green enrollment result by converting the spring kindergarten and grade 9 registration events into neighborhood-based Saturday enrollment clinics. Treat chronic absenteeism as the leading risk: assign each school a 50-student priority caseload from the SIS dashboard and require documented contact, barrier identification, and a return-to-school plan within 10 instructional days. Add a transportation check on every attendance plan, especially for families using Route 6, Route 14, and the temporary detour around Tidegate Avenue.

periods.analysis: This quarter moves us from yellow to red because chronic absenteeism climbed from 19.5% to 20.4%, and that is not a rounding error; it is a signal. K-12 Enrollment fell from 240500 to 238600 students, slipping below the >=240000 target into yellow, while safety incidents rose from 5.9 to 6.3 per 1,000 students and remain above the <=5 target. The end-of-year data showed a troubling concentration among ninth graders, multilingual newcomers, and students in temporary housing served through the Harbor Families office. I am concerned, but this is managed concern: we know the campuses, we know the students, and we have to move from broad encouragement to case-managed recovery.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a Red Attendance Response for the 40 campuses contributing the largest number of chronically absent students, with deputy superintendent check-ins every two weeks and public progress reviews by school. Rebuild enrollment by assigning re-engagement teams to the 1,900-student quarter-over-quarter decline, starting with no-show, withdrawal-pending, and address-unverified records. For safety, require each campus above 6 per 1,000 to run a June climate audit with student focus groups, hotspot maps, and corrective actions before summer programming begins.

periods.analysis: The red condition deepened: chronic absenteeism moved from 20.4% to 21%, and K-12 Enrollment declined from 238600 to 236667 students, still below the >=240000 target. Safety incidents also moved from 6.3 to 6.7 per 1,000 students, which tells me the start-of-year routines were not consistent enough across campuses. Our August roster reconciliation found large gaps in grades 8 to 10, especially in the Harbor East, Seaport, and Westline feeder patterns. The city is growing, but our schools are not automatically capturing that growth; we have to earn daily attendance and family confidence classroom by classroom.
periods.recommendations: Open the year with a 20-day attendance guarantee: every student absent twice in the first 10 days gets a same-week call and every student absent four times gets a home visit or community-site conference. Deploy mobile enrollment teams to apartment clusters near Airport Gateway, Pier 3, and Westline Station to recover students lost between 238600 and 236667. Stabilize safety by placing trained climate monitors at the 12 highest-incident middle and high schools during arrival, lunch, and dismissal until each site posts two consecutive weeks below its prior-quarter rate.

periods.analysis: We are still red, with chronic absenteeism rising from 21% to 21.5% and K-12 Enrollment falling from 236667 to 235000 students. Safety incidents held flat at 6.7 per 1,000 students, so we stopped the quarter-over-quarter increase, but flat is not good enough when the target is <=5. The attendance issue is now persistent across seasons, not just a back-to-school adjustment, and it is hitting hardest among students with prior-year chronic absence flags. The Harborview Attendance Exchange pilot at King, Salinas, and North Pier produced better family contact logs, but the scale is still too small for the size of the problem.
periods.recommendations: Expand the Harborview Attendance Exchange from 3 pilot schools to the full first cohort of 18 schools, with a shared script, barrier codes, and weekly superintendent review of completion rates. Pair the enrollment decline with a targeted “Still Harborview” campaign for students who transferred, withdrew without records, or missed registration, using evening call blocks and community partners at libraries and recreation centers. For safety, keep the incident plateau from becoming acceptance by requiring restorative-conference capacity at every school above 6 per 1,000 and adding substitute coverage so deans are visible during peak periods.

periods.analysis: The red status remains, and the enrollment measure has now moved into red: K-12 Enrollment dropped from 235000 to 233200 students against the >=240000 target. Chronic absenteeism increased from 21.5% to 21.8%, while safety incidents improved from 6.7 to 6.1 per 1,000 students, a real movement in the right direction but still above the <=5 target. The safety improvement followed the January reset at Harbor Tech, Bayview, and East Harbor High, where we tightened entry supervision and used student mediators before conflicts escalated. Attendance and enrollment, however, are now linked risks, and we cannot solve one without the other.
periods.recommendations: Move from school-by-school activity to a district attendance command structure, with one accountable owner for each feeder pattern and a weekly list of students who are both chronically absent and enrollment-unstable. Sustain the safety improvement by keeping the January reset through spring, including entry supervision, conflict mediation slots, and hotspot checks in restrooms, bus loops, and cafeterias. Recover enrollment by auditing every inactive record from the 235000 to 233200 decline and offering rapid re-entry appointments within 72 hours for families ready to return.

periods.analysis: We close this arc still in red: chronic absenteeism rose from 21.8% to 22%, and K-12 Enrollment declined from 233200 to 231500 students. Safety incidents moved slightly up from 6.1 to 6.2 per 1,000 students, so the winter improvement did not fully hold, though it remains better than the 6.7 level we saw in late 2025. The quarter shows an organization that is working hard but not yet changing the slope on attendance or enrollment. My read is plain: our safety systems are closer to control, while absenteeism has become the core instructional and equity threat.
periods.recommendations: Adopt a summer-to-fall recovery plan now, not in August: assign named staff to the top 5,000 chronically absent students, schedule family conferences before the last day of school, and confirm transportation, housing, and health barriers in the student record. Launch a July re-enrollment push at Portside Library, Airport Gateway Community Center, and the Seaport Family Resource Hub to address the drop from 233200 to 231500 students. For safety, preserve the practices that kept incidents below the prior 6.7 peak, but add a spring corrective plan for any campus above 7 per 1,000 with daily adult coverage maps and weekly incident review.

periods.analysis: Safety incidents improved to 6.0 per 1,000 students, but remain above target. Chronic absenteeism rose to 22.1% and enrollment declined to 230,900. Those two below-plan results outweigh the modest safety improvement.
periods.recommendations: Keep named attendance cases and re-enrollment follow-up visible in the next review while principals check first-term safety coverage.
